summary: Keiji Kanazawa opens by framing AI safety challenges: chatbots can be tricked into revealing unwanted information or bypassing safety measures through techniques like prefacing harmful queries with elaborate stories or spelling phrases backwards. He emphasizes 2025 as the year of agents, raising business concerns about AI manipulation. Drawing an analogy to traditional engineering, he argues that trust requires iterative building, checking, and testing, and stresses that trust is a team sport requiring collaboration between engineers and AI risk experts. Microsoft's AI red team, early pioneers in identifying GPT-3/GPT-4 vulnerabilities, built PyRIT (Python Risk Identification Toolkit). Azure AI Foundry offers a hosted version with an SDK and dashboard. Nagkumar demonstrates the tool with a RAG application on PostgreSQL running locally via Ollama, using a semantic kernel agent with a red team plugin that exposes functions for tool-calling into the red teaming process. The interactive mode shows the agent generating harmful prompts in specified categories, applying conversion strategies like base64 encoding, and sending them to the target. For end-to-end scans, users configure an AI project, select from four risk categories, specify the number of objectives, and choose attack strategies including combination strategies. Results showed GPT-4o with Azure guard rails resisting all attacks in a 160-query sample, while Llama 3 had 5 out of 40 successful attacks in hate and fairness. Direct model scans against GPT-4.1 without guard rails showed 25% success in violence and 20% in difficult complexity attacks; guard rails reduced success rates. In closing, Keiji situates red teaming within a broader engineering framework: first map anticipated risks for your application, implement guard rails initially, then run evaluations. Azure AI Foundry offers a suite of evaluators including quality checks, risk and safety classifiers (both input and output), agentic application evaluators, and support for custom evaluators. After red teaming reveals vulnerabilities, developers can apply guardrails such as content filters and prompt shields. During Q&A, the speakers clarify that guardrails operate outside the model itself—Azure AI Foundry provides input content filters and output content filters, and the raw model remains unchanged when filters are disabled. They share links to code and documentation and invite further questions at the Microsoft booth.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and AI Safety Motivation
sections.summary: Keiji Kanazawa introduces himself and Nagkumar, framing AI safety challenges with examples of tricking chatbots through narrative prefacing and backwards spelling. He emphasizes 2025 as the year of agents and draws an engineering analogy: engineers build trusted infrastructure through iterative testing, and AI requires the same discipline.

sections.title: Microsoft AI Red Team and PyRIT
sections.summary: Kanazawa introduces Microsoft's AI red team as pioneers in identifying LLM vulnerabilities. They built PyRIT, which Azure AI Foundry wraps in a hosted SDK with a dashboard for viewing evaluations, making red teaming accessible to AI engineers.

sections.title: Live Demo: Interactive Red Teaming Agent
sections.summary: Nagkumar demonstrates a RAG app on PostgreSQL via Ollama. The semantic kernel agent uses a red team plugin for tool-calling. Though live tool calling failed, he shows pre-run output demonstrating strategy selection, harmful prompt generation in violence category, base64 conversion, and target responses.

sections.title: End-to-End Scan Configuration and Results
sections.summary: Nagkumar shows scan setup: AI project configuration, four risk categories, number of objectives, and attack strategies including combination strategies. Pre-run results show GPT-4o with guard rails resisting all 160 attacks, while Llama 3 had 5/40 successes in hate and fairness.

sections.title: Direct Model Scan and Guard Rail Comparison
sections.summary: Nagkumar demonstrates direct model scanning against Azure OpenAI configurations. GPT-4.1 without guard rails showed 25% violence success and 20% difficult complexity success, including a Caesar encoding attack the assistant decoded. Guard rails on GPT-4.1 nano reduced attack success rates.

sections.title: Closing Framework, Guardrail Architecture, and Q&A
sections.summary: Keiji situates red teaming within a broader engineering framework: map risks first, implement guard rails, then evaluate. Azure AI Foundry offers quality evaluators, risk/safety classifiers (input and output), agentic evaluators, and custom evaluator support. Mitigations include content filters and prompt shields. In Q&A, the speakers clarify that guardrails are external to the raw model, providing both input and output content filtering. They share code and documentation links and invite questions at the Microsoft booth.
